- The current publications style sheet in /workspace/editorial/ governs copy, terminology, data presentation and sourcing. Fellows' outlines set the argument; the style sheet governs how it is presented.

# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".
B3. Headline toll: 46,728 "killed by gun violence". The fall campaign does not break deaths out by intent.
B4. Mass shootings: GVA's 656 for 2023, as "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston".
B5. Assault weapons: series line is "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings".
B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

 In recent months, gun violence has unfolded in everyday settings with assault weapons. In Austin, a man armed with an AR-style rifle opened fire in a crowded nightlife district, killing three people and injuring more than a dozen in minutes. 1 Andrew Weber and Chelsey Zhu, “Austin Police Release Video, Audio from Officers and Bystanders at West Sixth Street Shooting,” KUT 90.5 , updated March 9, 2026, https://www.kut.org/crime-justice/2026-03-05/austin-tx-west-sixth-street-shooting-bufords-apd-fbi-updates . Yarbrough Accidentally Shot by 6-Year-Old Brother in Home,” Alabama Daily News , March 24, 2026, https://aldailynews.com/teen-son-of-rep-yarbrough-accidentally-shot-by-6-year-old-brother-in-home . 

 Following the expiration of the federal assault weapons ban, 4 Public Law 103-322, Title XI (1994). Part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994, the Public Safety and Recreational Firearms Act prohibited semiautomatic assault weapons designated by specific make or model or by a combination of specific characteristics, such as a folding or telescopic stock or a pistol grip that extends below the action of the weapon (former 18 USC § 921(a)(30)(B)). It also prohibited ammunition magazines with more than 10 rounds, with exemptions for those lawfully possessed on or before the law’s enactment (former 18 USC § 921(31)). The law took effect September 13, 1994, and expired on September 13, 2004. Vivian S. Chu, “Federal Assault Weapons Ban: Legal Issues,” Congressional Research Service, February 14, 2013, https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/R42957.pdf . the use of deadly assault weapons and high-capacity magazines has surged on the United States’ streets, in its communities, and at the sites of its deadliest mass shootings. The gun industry’s marketing of firearms designed for military use to civilian consumers—particularly young men and children—has helped fuel the rise in the manufacture and sale of these weapons and magazines. 5  Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund“Assault Weapons and High-Capacity Magazines,” The Smoking Gun , https://smokinggun.org/assault-weapons-and-high-capacity-magazines . As the gun industry continues to profit, communities across the country pay the price. 

 Assault weapons and high-capacity magazines enable shooters to fire rapidly and inflict mass casualties in seconds. Although often characterized as weapons used only in high-profile mass shootings, evidence shows that assault weapons are increasingly recovered at the scenes of everyday violence in our country. Whether used in targeted crime, school shootings, or escalating arguments, they pose a danger beyond those of other firearms. Despite the unique lethality and the devastating toll these weapons inflict on our communities, there has been no federal restriction on their access or possession for more than two decades, and laws in only some states prohibit assault weapons and/or high-capacity magazines . Research shows that such regulations can save lives by reducing the risk of mass shootings and firearm violence overall.

 The research in this report demonstrates the inherent dangers of assault weapons and high-capacity magazines, examines the policies that have addressed them, and highlights the ways these weapons affect our nation’s gun violence epidemic beyond high-profile mass shootings. This analysis draws on Everytown for Gun Safety’s tracking of mass shooting incidents, 6 Everytown Research has historically tracked incidents of mass shootings in which four or more people, excluding the shooter, are killed in a single event, derived from the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s definition of a mass murder. In the analyses in this report, we examine mass shootings that meet this definition and occurred in the United States from 2016 to 2025. The data in this analysis is based on reviewing media and law enforcement sources, including incident reports, investigative reports, available court records, and historical criminal records. While there is no universally accepted definition of a mass shooting, and definitions vary considerably across research and data sources, this definition includes shootings of high public interest and allows for the examination of the firearm and magazine type in incidents that otherwise includes a high degree of missingness under more expansive definitions of mass shootings. Of the 230 mass shooting incidents we examine, at least one firearm type was identified in 131 incidents, and magazine type was identified in 54 incidents. decades of research on firearm violence, and The Smoking Gun . 7 Everytown for Gun Safety Support Fund, The Smoking Gun, https://smokinggun.org . The Smoking Gun is an online resource committed to exposing the gun industry’s role in our gun violence epidemic today through news stories, in-depth research, profiles on firearm manufacturers and suppliers, data, and more.
 As assault weapons appear in more shootings and at more crime scenes, the country faces an urgent need to enact new restrictions on assault weapons and high-capacity magazines to prevent further harms.

 Background checks for gun purchases are designed to prevent access to guns by convicted felons and other prohibited possessors. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act (the Brady Act), which went into effect in 1994, requires background checks on gun sales by licensed dealers (18 U.S.C. 922) but not on private sales or transfers of firearms (such as gifts). As of January 1, 2025, 19 states and the District of Columbia have comprehensive background check laws that apply to all firearm sales, although there are notable differences in these laws. For example, some states require that almost all firearm transfers to individuals occur through licensed dealers, who conduct background checks. Other states require background checks before law enforcement can issue a permit to purchase. Additional states have universal background check requirements that apply only to handguns or to handguns and some semiautomatic rifles.

 Summary of Evidence for How Background Checks Affect Outcomes

 We systematically reviewed scientific evidence on background checks to understand how these policies affect different outcomes in the United States.

 Evidence Strength for Background Checks

 Evidence is categorized as inconclusive, limited, moderate, or supportive. For some outcomes, not enough research met our inclusion criteria to assess the strength of evidence for the effects of background checks. An absence of evidence does not mean that background checks have no effect on those outcomes.

{"content": "# Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | NPI-PUB-2026-0457**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline Oct. 21; publication Oct. 27, 2026.*

## Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, one every 11 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- Two gaps in federal law help keep the toll this high: background checks are not required on gun sales outside the licensed dealer system, and the federal assault weapons ban expired in 2004.
- Congress can close both gaps: pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States. That works out to 128 people on an average day, one every 11 minutes, all year long. The annual count has eased somewhat from its pandemic-era peak. It remains a level of loss that no comparable nation tolerates for a single month.

Numbers this large go numb quickly, so it helps to slow them down. Every 11 minutes, somewhere in America, a family gets the call. The hospital room, the lockdown drill, the vigil at the school fence: gun violence on this scale is not a run of unthinkable anomalies. It is the ordinary background noise of American life, and it is the direct product of policy choices.

Two of those choices are squarely before Congress, and both have an evidence base behind them. The first is the refusal to require a background check on every gun sale. The second is the decision to let the federal assault weapons ban lapse in 2004, which returned military-patterned rifles and high-capacity magazines to the civilian market. Neither gap exists because Congress studied the problem and concluded these policies fail. Both exist because the votes were never there. The votes should be.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll starts young. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed in the United States, according to an analysis of federal mortality data by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death overall for young people, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer. For children and teens ages 1 to 19, the rate of deaths from gun violence pooled across 2021 through 2023 was 5.9 per 100,000. The United States stands alone among peer nations in letting firearms be the leading cause of child mortality at all.

No statistic conveys what that means. There is the classmate who notices the empty desk. There is the team that plays shorthanded. There are the parents who taught a 7-year-old the difference between a fire drill and the other kind. Grief on this scale is not an abstraction for American children; it is part of the curriculum.

The policies in this brief are not primarily youth policies, and they would not prevent every one of those deaths. They would prevent some of them, and they would do so with the smallest possible intrusion on lawful gun ownership: a check that takes minutes, and a ban on a class of weapons built to kill many people quickly.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994 the Brady Act has required a background check on gun sales by federally licensed dealers. It has never required one anywhere else. A sale arranged online between strangers, a purchase from a private seller at a gun show, a transfer in a parking lot: under federal law, none of these requires a background check. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have closed the gap for themselves. Congress has not.

How big is the gap? A 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among owners who bought privately, from someone other than a store or a pawnshop, half acquired the gun with no check at all. The unlicensed share of the market has been visible for decades: a 1994 national survey found roughly 40 percent of gun acquisitions took place without going through a licensed dealer, a figure that includes private sales as well as gifts and inheritances. Whatever the precise share today, millions of acquisitions sit outside the check system every year.

The evidence that checks matter is real. The most rigorous synthesis of the research, the RAND Corporation's ongoing review of gun policy evidence, finds moderate evidence that background check requirements reduce total homicides and firearm homicides. Universal background checks are also the narrowest possible ask: they do not stop a single lawful sale, they simply require that every sale confirm what federal law already presumes, that the buyer is not a prohibited person.

The gap is not an accident of drafting. It is a maintained exemption, and it is maintained against the weight of public opinion, with decades of polling showing large majorities, including gun owners, supporting checks on all sales.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Americans know the cost of this gap by heart, as a list of place names. Parkland, Florida, in 2018. Uvalde, Texas, in 2022. Lewiston, Maine, in October 2023, where a shooter killed 18 people in a single evening. In each of those attacks, the shooter used a semi-automatic rifle of the kind the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Counts and definitions matter here, so it is worth stating them plainly. The Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter, counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692. Even on the narrowest definition, four or more people killed, the AP/USA Today/Northeastern database counted 36 mass killings in 2023.

Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings. By assault weapons, this brief means the class of semi-automatic firearms patterned on military designs, together with the high-capacity magazines that feed them. In 44 high-fatality mass shootings between 1981 and 2017, assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 people killed, or 86 percent, according to a peer-reviewed analysis in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery. When these weapons are in the picture, the carnage compounds: Everytown's analysis of mass shootings from 2016 through 2025 found roughly four times as many people shot in incidents involving an assault weapon or high-capacity magazine as in incidents involving neither.

Critics of a new ban raise an objection that deserves a straight answer. Rifles of all kinds, they note, are used in a small share of American murders: 2.6 percent in 2017, and 297 murders in 2018, about 2 percent of the total, according to the FBI, which does not separate AR-style rifles from hunting rifles in its data. That is true, and it does not change what a mass-shooting policy is for. The question is not how often rifles are used to kill; it is what they are used for when they are. Handguns are used in more mass shootings overall. The deadliest ones run on assault weapons, and the difference shows up in the body count: 86 percent of deaths in the high-fatality incidents researchers have analyzed, and four times the casualties when one is used. A murder count cannot measure the difference between a shooting that ends when a magazine is empty and one that ends when a SWAT team arrives.

The federal ban was in force from September 1994 to September 2004. During those years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the periods before and after, the same peer-reviewed analysis found. The original law was narrow: it covered a defined list of weapons and limited magazines to 10 rounds, and manufacturers evaded it with cosmetic redesigns after it expired. A new ban should be written for the market as it exists now, covering the copycat models and the high-capacity magazines that multiply every death toll in this section.

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online gaps in the Brady framework, and fund enforcement so the requirement is real in practice.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the prohibitions in force from 1994 to 2004 and extend them to the copycat rifles and high-capacity magazines the industry designed to evade the original law.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, so prevention policy rests on evidence rather than on a research field that Congress starved for two decades.
4. **Support state extreme-risk laws.** Fund grant programs that help states adopt, implement and enforce extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis.

Congress has closed harder gaps than these, and it has done so against the same predictions of futility. The toll in this brief, 46,728 people in a single year, is not a fact of nature. It is the current setting of American policy, and Congress can change it.

*Data and source lines for every figure in this brief appear in the accompanying data appendix.*

The toll starts young. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death overall for young people, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer. These policies would not prevent every one of those deaths. They would prevent some of them, with the smallest possible intrusion on lawful gun ownership: a check that takes minutes, and a ban on weapons built to kill many people quickly.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994 the Brady Act has required a background check on gun sales by federally licensed dealers. It has never required one anywhere else. A sale arranged online between strangers, a purchase from a private seller at a gun show, a transfer in a parking lot: under federal law, none of these requires a background check. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have moved to close the gap for themselves. Congress has not.

How big is the gap? A 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among owners who bought privately, from someone other than a store or a pawnshop, half acquired the gun with no check at all. The unlicensed share of the market has been visible for decades: a 1994 national survey found roughly 40 percent of gun acquisitions took place without going through a licensed dealer, a figure that includes private sales as well as gifts and inheritances. Whatever the precise share today, millions of acquisitions sit outside the check system every year.

The evidence that checks matter is real. The most rigorous synthesis of the research, the RAND Corporation's ongoing review of gun policy evidence, finds moderate evidence that background check requirements reduce total homicides and firearm homicides. Checks are also the narrowest possible ask: they stop no lawful sale, they simply confirm what federal law already presumes, that the buyer is not a prohibited person.

The gap is not an accident of drafting. It is a maintained exemption, held against the weight of public opinion: large majorities, gun owners included, have supported checks on all sales for years.

Americans know the cost of mass shootings by heart, as a list of place names. Parkland, Florida, in 2018. Uvalde, Texas, in 2022. In each of those attacks, the shooter used a semi-automatic rifle of the kind the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Counts and definitions matter here. The Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter, counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692. Even on the narrowest definition, four or more people killed, the AP/USA Today/Northeastern database counted 36 mass killings in 2023.

Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings. By assault weapons, this brief means the class of semi-automatic firearms patterned on military designs, together with the high-capacity magazines that feed them. In 44 high-fatality mass shootings between 1981 and 2017, assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 people killed, or 86 percent, according to a peer-reviewed analysis in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery. When these weapons are in the picture, the carnage compounds: Everytown's analysis of mass shootings from 2016 through 2025 found roughly four times as many people shot in incidents involving an assault weapon or high-capacity magazine as in incidents involving neither.

Rifles of all kinds, they note, are used in a small share of American murders: 2.6 percent in 2017, and 297 murders in 2018, about 2 percent of the total, according to the FBI, which does not separate AR-style rifles from hunting rifles in its data. That is true, and it does not change what a mass-shooting policy is for. The question is not how often rifles are used to kill; it is what they are used for when they are. Handguns are used in more mass shootings overall. The deadliest ones run on assault weapons, and the difference shows up in the body count: 86 percent of deaths in the high-fatality incidents researchers have analyzed, and four times the casualties when one is used. A murder rate cannot measure the difference between a shooting that ends when a magazine is empty and one that ends when a SWAT team arrives.

The federal ban was in force from September 1994 to September 2004. During those years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the periods before and after, the same peer-reviewed analysis found. The original law was narrow, covering a defined list of weapons and limiting magazines to 10 rounds, and manufacturers evaded it with cosmetic redesigns after it expired. A new ban should be written for the market as it exists now, covering the copycats and the high-capacity magazines that multiply every death toll above.

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online gaps in the Brady framework, and fund enforcement so the requirement is real in practice.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the prohibitions in force from 1994 to 2004 and extend them to the copycat rifles and high-capacity magazines the industry designed to evade the original law.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, so prevention policy rests on evidence rather than on a research field that Congress starved for two decades.
4. **Support state extreme-risk laws.** Fund grant programs that help states adopt, implement and enforce extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis.

Congress has closed harder gaps against the same predictions of futility. The toll in this brief, 46,728 people in a single year, is not a fact of nature. It is the current setting of American policy, and Congress can change it.

# Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | NPI-PUB-2026-0457**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline Oct. 21; publication Oct. 27, 2026.*

## Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, one every 11 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Two gaps in federal law help keep the toll this high: background checks are not required on gun sales outside the licensed dealer system, and the federal assault weapons ban expired in 2004.
- Congress can close both gaps: pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States. That works out to 128 people on an average day, one every 11 minutes, all year long. The annual count has eased somewhat from its pandemic-era peak. It remains a level of loss that no comparable nation tolerates for a single month.

Numbers this large go numb quickly, so it helps to slow them down. Every 11 minutes, somewhere in America, a family gets the call. The hospital room, the lockdown drill, the vigil at the school fence: gun violence on this scale is not a run of unthinkable anomalies. It is the ordinary background noise of American life, and it is the direct product of policy choices.

Two of those choices are squarely before Congress. The first is the refusal to require a background check on every gun sale. The second is the decision to let the federal assault weapons ban lapse in 2004, returning military-patterned rifles and high-capacity magazines to the civilian market. Neither gap reflects a finding that these policies fail. Both persist because the votes were never there. The votes should be.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll starts young. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed in the United States, according to an analysis of federal mortality data by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death overall for young people, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer. For children and teens ages 1 to 19, the rate of deaths from gun violence pooled across 2021 through 2023 was 5.9 per 100,000. The United States stands alone among peer nations in letting firearms be the leading cause of child mortality at all.

No statistic conveys what that means. There is the classmate who notices the empty desk. There is the team that plays shorthanded. There are the parents who taught a 7-year-old the difference between a fire drill and the other kind. Grief on this scale is not an abstraction for American children; it is part of the curriculum.

These po
... [3327 chars truncated] ...
e picture, the carnage compounds: Everytown's analysis of mass shootings from 2016 through 2025 found roughly four times as many people shot in incidents involving an assault weapon or high-capacity magazine as in incidents involving neither.

Critics of a new ban raise an objection that deserves a straight answer. Rifles of all kinds, they note, are used in a small share of American murders: 2.6 percent in 2017, and 297 murders in 2018, about 2 percent of the total, according to the FBI, which does not separate AR-style rifles from hunting rifles in its data. That is true, and it does not change what a mass-shooting policy is for. The question is not how often rifles are used to kill; it is what they are used for when they are. Handguns are used in more mass shootings overall. The deadliest ones run on assault weapons, and the difference shows up in the body count: 86 percent of deaths in the high-fatality incidents researchers have analyzed, and four times the casualties when one is used. A murder rate cannot measure the difference between a shooting that ends when a magazine is empty and one that ends when a SWAT team arrives.

The federal ban was in force from September 1994 to September 2004. During those years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the periods before and after, the same peer-reviewed analysis found. The original law was narrow, covering a defined list of weapons and limiting magazines to 10 rounds, and manufacturers evaded it with cosmetic redesigns after it expired. A new ban should be written for the market as it exists now, covering the copycats and the high-capacity magazines that multiply every death toll above.

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online gaps in the Brady framework, and fund enforcement so the requirement is real in practice.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the prohibitions in force from 1994 to 2004 and extend them to the copycat rifles and high-capacity magazines the industry designed to evade the original law.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, so prevention policy rests on evidence rather than on a research field that Congress starved for two decades.
4. **Support state extreme-risk laws.** Fund grant programs that help states adopt, implement and enforce extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|

# Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | NPI-PUB-2026-0457**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline Oct. 21; publication Oct. 27, 2026.*

## Executive summary

- In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, one every 11 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Two gaps in federal law help keep the toll this high: background checks are not required on gun sales outside the licensed dealer system, and the federal assault weapons ban expired in 2004.
- Congress can close both gaps: pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States. That works out to 128 people on an average day, one every 11 minutes, all year long. The annual count has eased somewhat from its pandemic-era peak. It remains a level of loss that no comparable nation tolerates for a single month.

Numbers this large go numb quickly, so it helps to slow them down. Every 11 minutes, somewhere in America, a family gets the call. The hospital room, the lockdown drill, the vigil at the school fence: gun violence on this scale is not a run of unthinkable anomalies. It is the ordinary background noise of American life, and it is the direct product of policy choices.

Two of those choices are squarely before Congress. The first is the refusal to require a background check on every gun sale. The second is the decision to let the federal assault weapons ban lapse in 2004, returning military-patterned rifles and high-capacity magazines to the civilian market. Neither gap reflects a finding that these policies fail. Both persist because the votes were never there. The votes should be.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll starts young. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed in the United States, according to an analysis of federal mortality data by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death overall for young people, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer. For children and teens ages 1 to 19, the rate of deaths from gun violence pooled across 2021 through 2023 was 5.9 per 100,000. The United States stands alone among peer nations in letting firearms be the leading cause of child mortality at all.

No statistic conveys what that means. There is the classmate who notices the empty desk. There is the team that plays shorthanded. There are the parents who taught a 7-year-old the difference between a fire drill and the other kind. Grief on this scale is not an abstraction for American children; it is part of the curriculum.

These policies would not prevent every one of those deaths. They would prevent some of them, with the smallest possible intrusion on lawful gun ownership: a check that takes minutes, and a ban on weapons built to kill many people quickly.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994 the Brady Act has required a background check on gun sales by federally licensed dealers. It has never required one anywhere else. A sale arranged online between strangers, a purchase from a private seller at a gun show, a transfer in a parking lot: under federal law, none of these requires a background check. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have moved to close the gap for themselves. Congress has not.

How big is the gap? A 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that 22 percent of owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among owners who bought privately, from someone other than a store or a pawnshop, half acquired the gun with no check at all. The unlicensed share of the market has been visible for decades: a 1994 national survey found roughly 40 percent of gun acquisitions took place without going through a licensed dealer, a figure that includes private sales as well as gifts and inheritances. Whatever the precise share today, millions of acquisitions sit outside the check system every year.

The evidence that checks matter is real. The most rigorous synthesis of the research, the RAND Corporation's ongoing review of gun policy evidence, finds moderate evidence that background check requirements reduce total homicides and firearm homicides. Checks are also the narrowest possible ask: they stop no lawful sale, they simply confirm what federal law already presumes, that the buyer is not a prohibited person.

The gap is not an accident of drafting. It is a maintained exemption, held against the weight of public opinion: large majorities, gun owners included, have supported checks on all sales for years.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Americans know the cost of mass shootings by heart, as a list of place names. Parkland, Florida, in 2018. Uvalde, Texas, in 2022. Lewiston, Maine, in October 2023, where a shooter killed 18 people in a single evening. In each of those attacks, the shooter used a semi-automatic rifle of the kind the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Counts and definitions matter here. The Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter, counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692. Even on the narrowest definition, four or more people killed, the AP/USA Today/Northeastern database counted 36 mass killings in 2023 through late October.

Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's deadliest mass shootings. By assault weapons, this brief means the class of semi-automatic firearms patterned on military designs, together with the high-capacity magazines that feed them. In 44 high-fatality mass shootings between 1981 and 2017, assault rifles accounted for 430 of the 501 people killed, or 86 percent, according to a peer-reviewed analysis in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery. When these weapons are in the picture, the carnage compounds: Everytown's analysis of mass shootings from 2016 through 2025 found roughly four times as many people shot in incidents involving an assault weapon or high-capacity magazine as in incidents involving neither.

Critics of a new ban raise an objection that deserves a straight answer. Rifles of all kinds, they note, are used in a small share of American murders: 2.6 percent in 2017, and 297 murders in 2018, about 2 percent of the total, according to the FBI, which does not separate AR-style rifles from hunting rifles in its data. That is true, and it does not change what a mass-shooting policy is for. The question is not how often rifles are used to kill; it is what they are used for when they are. Handguns are used in more mass shootings overall. The deadliest ones run on assault weapons, and the difference shows up in the body count: 86 percent of deaths in the high-fatality incidents researchers have analyzed, and four times the casualties when one is used. A murder rate cannot measure the difference between a shooting that ends when a magazine is empty and one that ends when a SWAT team arrives.

The federal ban was in force from September 1994 to September 2004. During those years, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely than in the periods before and after, the same peer-reviewed analysis found. The original law was narrow, covering a defined list of weapons and limiting magazines to 10 rounds, and manufacturers evaded it with cosmetic redesigns after it expired. A new ban should be written for the market as it exists now, covering the copycats and the high-capacity magazines that multiply every death toll above.

## 5. Recommendations for Congress

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, closing the private-sale, gun-show and online gaps in the Brady framework, and fund enforcement so the requirement is real in practice.
2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the prohibitions in force from 1994 to 2004 and extend them to the copycat rifles and high-capacity magazines the industry designed to evade the original law.
3. **Fund gun violence research.** Appropriate sustained, dedicated funding for gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, so prevention policy rests on evidence rather than on a research field that Congress starved for two decades.
4. **Support state extreme-risk laws.** Fund grant programs that help states adopt, implement and enforce extreme-risk laws, which allow families and law enforcement to petition a court to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis.

Congress has closed harder gaps against the same predictions of futility. The toll in this brief, 46,728 people in a single year, is not a fact of nature. It is the current setting of American policy, and Congress can change it.

*Data and source lines for every figure in this brief appear in the accompanying data appendix.*

## Key statistics

1. **46,728** Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023, one every 11 minutes.
   *Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.*

2. **2,566** children and teens ages 1 to 17 were shot and killed in 2023.

4. The gun death rate for children and teens ages 1 to 19 was **5.9 per 100,000**, pooled across 2021 through 2023.
   *Source: Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research.*

   *Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.*

   *Source: Cook and Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, 1994.*

7. **656 mass shootings** in 2023, incidents in which four or more people were shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter: **712 killed, 2,692 injured**.
   *Source: Gun Violence Archive, Mass Shootings in 2023.*

   *Source: DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019.*

## What the brief recommends

- **Pass universal background checks** on every firearm sale and transfer.
- **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban**, covering copycat rifles and high-capacity magazines.

# EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET

**NPI-PUB-2026-0457 | Draft for review**

Media contact: NPI Office of Communications, [details to be added]

## New NPI brief calls on Congress to close two gaps in federal gun law

WASHINGTON, D.C., Oct. 27, 2026. The Northgate Progress Institute today published Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: the case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," calling on Congress to pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the federal assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research and support state extreme-risk laws.

The brief, by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, senior fellow for gun violence prevention, documents the cost of two federal policy gaps. In 2023, 46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence, one every 11 minutes. Guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17, with 2,566 young people shot and killed. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, incidents in which four or more people were shot, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692.

Federal law requires background checks only for sales by licensed dealers. A 2015 national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a check. The federal assault weapons ban has been expired since 2004; during its years in force, mass-shooting fatalities were 70 percent less likely, a peer-reviewed analysis found.

"Our gun laws have two gaps that most peer nations closed long ago," Whitfield said. "One lets guns change hands with no background check at all. The other put military-style rifles and high-capacity magazines back on the civilian market in 2004. Congress can close both this year, and with 128 Americans killed by gun violence every day, the cost of waiting is being paid in lives."

The brief and data appendix are on the NPI website.

The Northgate Progress Institute is a Washington, D.C., policy institute working for safer, more equitable communities through evidence-based policy. Safer Communities is NPI's gun violence prevention brief series.
